contributions.headingText: Mucosal melanoma is a malignant melanocytic neoplasm arising within the female genital tract in a non-cutaneous site, usually in the vulva or vagina and rarely in the cervix.
Acceptable: mucosal melanoma; mucosal lentiginous melanoma; vaginal melanoma; vulvar melanoma; vulvovaginal melanoma
Desmoplastic melanoma; nodular melanoma; mucosal lentiginous melanoma
These uncommon tumours mostly arise in mucosa of the vulva or vagina {15166669; 21293284; 25384702}. Rare cases arise in the cervix {30044323}.

Most patients are postmenopausal, with a median age of 65 years {25384702}. Symptoms and signs depend on the anatomical location and include the presence of a mass, a macule or a non-pigmented lesion, and/or bleeding {12409721}.

Primary melanoma accounts for approximately 5% of malignancies of the vulva and vagina. Vulvovaginal melanomas represent approximately 1% of all melanomas in most European populations but about 25% of melanomas in dark-skinned individuals {24272143}.
The etiology is unknown. Unlike cutaneous melanomas, mucosal melanomas have no association with ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure {28467829; 31320640}.

In contrast to cutaneous melanomas, mucosal melanomas show a low mutation burden, without a UV signature. Instead, they are characterized by numerous chromosomal structural variants and abundant copy-number changes, including multiple high-level amplifications {31320640; 30847022; 28467829; 23620124}. The most common somatic mutations involve SF3B1, KIT, ATRX, TP53, ARID2, SETD2, and BRAF (occurring at a lower frequency than in cutaneous melanomas) {28467829; 28720667}.

Mucosal vulvar melanomas usually present as pigmented plaques, but amelanotic ulcerated nodules are also common. Vaginal melanomas usually present as large, ulcerated, nodular masses and often involve the cervix. An associated naevus is rarely seen.

The tumour is usually formed by sheets or expansive nodules of large pleomorphic epithelioid or (less commonly) spindle malignant melanocytic cells. Necrosis is uncommon. The nuclei often have vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli. Occasionally, small or naevoid cells may predominate. Melanin production is variable but usually focally present within both melanoma cells and macrophages. Vulvar melanoma often shows a confluent nested and lentiginous growth pattern of the epidermal component, with pagetoid spread. In contrast, vaginal melanoma is typically characterized by a lentiginous growth of single atypical melanocytes in the basal epithelial layer, sometimes with nests or confluent growth. A subepithelial lymphocytic infiltrate is common. Immunohistochemically, there is usually reactivity of the tumour cells for S100, SOX10, HMB45, and melan-A (MART1) {12409721}.

Typically there is a non-cohesive population of large epithelioid or sometimes spindle cells {17276948}. Occasional giant cells and intranuclear pseudoinclusions are often present. Cytoplasmic pigment is usually present in a minority of cells. Pigmented macrophages may be seen in the background.
BRAF and KIT tumour mutation testing may be useful in patients for whom targeted therapies are being considered.

Essential: melanocytic tumour with malignant features.

Desirable: reactivity for melanocytic markers (if needed).

Vulvar melanoma is staged using the cutaneous melanoma staging system. There are no Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) staging criteria for melanomas occurring elsewhere in the female genital tract. However, it has been recommended that the cutaneous melanoma staging system should also be applied to vaginal melanomas {25384702}.

Unlike for patients with cutaneous melanoma, the overall survival for patients with primary melanoma of the female genital tract is relatively poor {29748886; 28600969}. This is partly attributable to delayed detection. Increased tumour thickness, ulceration, and high mitotic count are poor prognostic features in vulvovaginal melanoma {25384702; 27864417}. The reported 5-year survival rates for patients with vulvovaginal melanoma are approximately 20%. Data on outcomes after systemic immunotherapy for metastatic mucosal melanoma are limited, but the outcomes appear to be poorer than with cutaneous melanoma {27533633}.
